The position of the Prime Minister is not just a position to pronounce decisions, but also a position to publicly clarify the justification for the decisions made. There is a fundamental difference between giving a political answer to those who criticize the government and giving an institutional answer to the work done by the government. The prime minister's latest social media remarks have also sparked debate over the boundaries between political competition and national guardianship. On November 5, he commented on Facebook that "your workers fight, your leaders sit back and laugh," comparing the role of his leaders to trying to save the country. It was not clear who was being targeted in the remarks. But they have been interpreted as a dig at the old political parties. The Prime Minister also has the right to criticize the opposition party. But the Prime Minister's responsibility is broader than the role of the leader of a political group. A leader competing in an election can excite his party's supporters and show the weaknesses of the opposition. After becoming the Prime Minister, he has a constitutional and political responsibility towards all citizens. CPN-UML cadres are also Nepalis. Nepali Congress supporters are also Nepalis. Citizens affiliated with the Maoists, the RPP or any other political party have equal rights over this country. Citizens who are not affiliated with any political party are also members of the state with equal rights. The vote of a citizen who votes for the National Independent Party is as respectable as the vote of a citizen who does not vote for it. The statement that only those who support Balendra Shah are in favor of change and those who criticize him are against change cannot be accepted from a democratic perspective. National loyalty is not a matter that can be proven by supporting any political party. This is where the Prime Minister's responsibility for language becomes important. The sharp expressions used in political competition yesterday and the language used by the head of state after coming to power do not have the same effect. When the Prime Minister constantly emphasizes the political division as 'ours' and 'yours', it can create enthusiasm among supporters. But it can also create suspicion among citizens with different political views about how the state views itself. It is not possible to conclude from a single Facebook expression that the Prime Minister does not consider supporters of other parties to be citizens. But the dignity of public office certainly expects restraint and inclusiveness in political language. The leader of a political party seeks to unify his organization; the prime minister of a country must build a common national identity even among citizens who hold different views. This distinction between the two roles is a crucial test of democratic leadership. The guardianship of the prime minister does not mean agreeing with everyone, but also giving equal importance to the rights and dignity of those who disagree. Citizens who criticize the government are not enemies, but participants in the democratic process. Opposition parties are not anti-state organizations, but part of the constitutional structure that holds the government accountable through parliament. The weaknesses of the old political parties were serious and are not immune to criticism. The Congress, UML and Maoist leaderships that have been in power for a long time will also have to face many questions regarding administrative interference, political participation, poor service delivery and public accountability. Their past decisions need to be evaluated. But the weaknesses of the old parties cannot be the basis for justifying the new government's decisions. Just because other governments have politically interfered in police administration in the past does not mean that the current government can do the same. If the previous prime minister was absent from parliament, it is the responsibility of the new leadership to correct it. If the previous governments behaved intolerantly towards journalism, then the expectation of change is that they should not repeat it. Therefore, when assessing the achievements of a new government, it is not enough to simply ask whether it is more popular than the old party. The important questions are how much it has made state institutions independent, how transparent government decisions have been, what improvements have been made in public services, how accountable it has been to parliament, and what practices have been established in protecting civil rights. Popularity is political capital. But it is not a substitute for constitutional accountability. An electoral mandate is the basis for forming a government, not permission to operate all state institutions according to one's political will. The real achievement of political change lies not in the power of one person, but in the creation of institutions that function fairly even when individuals change. The foundation of good governance is strong in a state with a police force that can conduct impartial investigations even without the direction of the Prime Minister, an administration that works without political pressure, a journalism that can criticize government decisions, an executive that takes the questions of public representatives seriously, and a fearless judiciary. Conversely, if the entire administrative success starts to depend on the willpower of a single person, the long-term stability of such a system may be questioned. The questions that need to be answered by the Balen government are clear. Who ordered the arrest of the journalist and what was the legal justification for it? What is the factual basis for the different explanations from the Prime Minister’s Secretariat and the police? What was the objective basis for changing the role of the Inspector General of Police? Was there political interference in the investigation involving people close to power? When will a clear practice of holding the Prime Minister accountable through regular questions and answers in Parliament be established? Answering these questions is not about weakening the government; it is an opportunity to strengthen public trust and institutional legitimacy. Criticizing the government in a democracy is not about trying to make the government fail. The purpose of criticism is also to put pressure on it to correct wrong practices. Questioning the use of state power, journalists publishing news that is inconvenient for the government, MPs demanding answers from the Prime Minister, and police leadership having the legal basis of their decisions examined are natural processes in a democratic system. The government may be uncomfortable with these processes, but it is its responsibility to respect them. Ultimately, the question of good governance is not limited to the personal disputes of any one Prime Minister, Minister, Journalist or Inspector General of Police. It is a question of what kind of governance culture to establish in Nepal. It is a question of whether the new political leadership will repeat the weaknesses of the old system or establish different institutional practices. The people can change the political leadership, but the responsibility to strengthen the constitutional institutions must be borne by the leadership itself. Answering questions in parliament is good governance. Facing questions from journalists is good governance. Allowing the police to act according to the law is good governance. Respecting the rights of the opposition is good governance. Treating citizens who do not support you with equal respect is good governance. Being ready to correct your own decisions if they are wrong is also good governance. Good governance is not just the ability to discipline others, but also the commitment to keep your power under the discipline of the constitution and the law. The main question that needs to be asked of the Balen government now is this – is the character of governance changing with the change in power, or is the old tendency to use state power under the new slogan of good governance continuing? No Facebook status, political speech or propaganda campaign will answer this. The government's decision-making process, institutional behavior and public accountability will provide it. Because ultimately, the true identity of good governance in a democracy is not determined by how powerful the government is, but by how justly, legitimately and responsibly that power is used.

The same question became more serious when the police took three journalists into custody on October 30. An attempt was also made to take Naya Patrika journalist Nawaraj Mainali from his office. The Federation of Nepali Journalists and the Press Council objected to the incident. What is special is that the police explanation included the concern expressed by the Prime Minister's Office. However, the Prime Minister's Secretariat said that there was no instruction or prior information. The Secretariat claimed that the Prime Minister had instructed to release the journalists immediately after learning about it, and they were released that evening.

Who lied here? The conclusion cannot be drawn without adequate investigation. But the government's responsibility does not end with issuing a press release. If the police summoned the journalist in the interest of the Prime Minister's Office, what was the legal basis for it? If the office had no involvement, why did the police give such an explanation? How was the need to take the journalist under control established? If the police were mobilized incorrectly, how was the accountability of the concerned officer determined? A government that claims good governance should give formal and evidence-based answers to such questions. Merely releasing the journalist after arrest is not a sufficient institutional solution.

Along with these incidents, the case of Inspector General of Police Dan Bahadur Karki has sparked another serious debate about the autonomy of state institutions. An emergency cabinet meeting held on November 4 removed Karki from the post of Inspector General of Police and made him the Prime Minister's Special Security Advisor, and appointed Manoj Kumar KC as the new police chief. The government has clarified that this is not an action but a change of responsibility. The government has the right to manage administrative leadership within the limits given by law. However, the legal basis and administrative necessity for an emergency change in the leadership of the country's main security agency need to be made public.

Karki's departure It has been claimed that there was a difference of opinion between the Prime Minister's Secretariat and the police leadership regarding the investigation into Inam Sapkota and the directive to immediately arrest various individuals. These details have not been verified by an independent judicial review. Karki's police leadership was also criticized and accused of work performance, procurement processes and other issues. Therefore, it is not appropriate to portray this dispute as an incident where one side is completely right and the other is completely wrong. But if the police chief says that a legal basis is necessary to arrest someone, then it raises serious questions about the rule of law. The first responsibility of the police is not to fulfill the wishes of the political leadership, but to act according to the law.

The most important aspect of this case is that Karki has filed a writ petition in the Supreme Court against the government's decision. In the writ petition filed on November 6, he has questioned the legal basis and process of the decision to remove him. Its hearing is scheduled for November 16. The final decision is yet to come from the court. But the fact that an Inspector General of Police has to go to the Supreme Court to review the legality of his exit is in itself reason enough to publicly debate the government's decision-making process. The question is not only about saving Karki's position, but also about the criteria under which the administrative power used against a police chief today will be used against any other public official tomorrow.

An incident that took place in a parliamentary committee a few months ago adds another meaning to this dispute. During a discussion in the Public Accounts Committee on allegations related to the purchase of police uniforms, Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS) MP Khagendra Sunar had strongly questioned the Inspector General of Police. Then, Home Minister Sudan Gurung said that no one should act as a judge and convict another person based solely on allegations. That statement contained a sound legal principle – allegations and proven crimes are not the same thing. But this principle should be applied equally to executive decisions.

The government, which reminds MPs not to become judges, should also ensure that its own ministers, the Prime Minister's Secretariat, or the political leadership do not violate the boundaries of the investigation and judicial process. The principles of good governance cannot be changed according to individuals.

Not only this, the question of how accountable the Prime Minister himself is to the Parliament is also equally important. It has been made public that Prime Minister Balendra Shah attended only 6 meetings out of the 68 meetings of the second session of the House of Representatives and only once in the National Assembly. There has also been criticism that the regular Q&A with the Prime Minister was not conducted effectively and that the answers sought by the MPs on various national issues were not received. It is not mandatory for the Prime Minister to attend every parliamentary meeting. He has executive responsibilities and other tasks of national importance. But in a parliamentary democracy, the government is accountable to the Parliament.

Article 76(10) of the Constitution of Nepal also provides that the Prime Minister and ministers are collectively responsible to the Federal Parliament. Therefore, appearing in Parliament and answering questions from public representatives is not a political favor, but an exercise of constitutional responsibility.

In this context, the Prime Minister's style of public communication cannot be ignored. Balendra Shah, who has been making his views public through social media since he was the mayor of Kathmandu Metropolitan City, has been criticized for prioritizing personal social media over direct press conferences and regular institutional dialogues even after becoming Prime Minister. Using social media is not wrong. It has importance as a means of direct communication with citizens. But Facebook status and public accountability are not the same thing. One can express opinions on topics that seem favorable to one on Facebook. But one must face uncomfortable questions in a press conference. One must answer questions asked by people's representatives in parliament in a legal manner.

Questions raised by independent media about government decisions cannot be addressed solely through personal status. Why doesn't the Prime Minister, who can respond to opposition party leaders on social media, give equal importance to answering questions from the people's representatives of those same parties in Parliament? If the main basis of good governance is accountability, shouldn't the person leading the government set an example by practicing accountability himself? The position of the Prime Minister is not just a position to pronounce decisions, but also a position to publicly clarify the justification for the decisions made. There is a fundamental difference between giving a political answer to those who criticize the government and giving an institutional answer to the work done by the government.

The prime minister's latest social media remarks have also sparked debate over the boundaries between political competition and national guardianship. On November 5, he commented on Facebook that "your workers fight, your leaders sit back and laugh," comparing the role of his leaders to trying to save the country. It was not clear who was being targeted in the remarks. But they have been interpreted as a dig at the old political parties.

The Prime Minister also has the right to criticize the opposition party. But the Prime Minister's responsibility is broader than the role of the leader of a political group. A leader competing in an election can excite his party's supporters and show the weaknesses of the opposition. After becoming the Prime Minister, he has a constitutional and political responsibility towards all citizens.

CPN-UML cadres are also Nepalis. Nepali Congress supporters are also Nepalis. Citizens affiliated with the Maoists, the RPP or any other political party have equal rights over this country. Citizens who are not affiliated with any political party are also members of the state with equal rights. The vote of a citizen who votes for the National Independent Party is as respectable as the vote of a citizen who does not vote for it. The statement that only those who support Balendra Shah are in favor of change and those who criticize him are against change cannot be accepted from a democratic perspective. National loyalty is not a matter that can be proven by supporting any political party.

This is where the Prime Minister's responsibility for language becomes important. The sharp expressions used in political competition yesterday and the language used by the head of state after coming to power do not have the same effect. When the Prime Minister constantly emphasizes the political division as 'ours' and 'yours', it can create enthusiasm among supporters. But it can also create suspicion among citizens with different political views about how the state views itself. It is not possible to conclude from a single Facebook expression that the Prime Minister does not consider supporters of other parties to be citizens. But the dignity of public office certainly expects restraint and inclusiveness in political language.

The leader of a political party seeks to unify his organization; the prime minister of a country must build a common national identity even among citizens who hold different views. This distinction between the two roles is a crucial test of democratic leadership. The guardianship of the prime minister does not mean agreeing with everyone, but also giving equal importance to the rights and dignity of those who disagree. Citizens who criticize the government are not enemies, but participants in the democratic process. Opposition parties are not anti-state organizations, but part of the constitutional structure that holds the government accountable through parliament.

The weaknesses of the old political parties were serious and are not immune to criticism. The Congress, UML and Maoist leaderships that have been in power for a long time will also have to face many questions regarding administrative interference, political participation, poor service delivery and public accountability. Their past decisions need to be evaluated. But the weaknesses of the old parties cannot be the basis for justifying the new government's decisions. Just because other governments have politically interfered in police administration in the past does not mean that the current government can do the same. If the previous prime minister was absent from parliament, it is the responsibility of the new leadership to correct it. If the previous governments behaved intolerantly towards journalism, then the expectation of change is that they should not repeat it.

Therefore, when assessing the achievements of a new government, it is not enough to simply ask whether it is more popular than the old party. The important questions are how much it has made state institutions independent, how transparent government decisions have been, what improvements have been made in public services, how accountable it has been to parliament, and what practices have been established in protecting civil rights. Popularity is political capital. But it is not a substitute for constitutional accountability. An electoral mandate is the basis for forming a government, not permission to operate all state institutions according to one's political will.

The real achievement of political change lies not in the power of one person, but in the creation of institutions that function fairly even when individuals change. The foundation of good governance is strong in a state with a police force that can conduct impartial investigations even without the direction of the Prime Minister, an administration that works without political pressure, a journalism that can criticize government decisions, an executive that takes the questions of public representatives seriously, and a fearless judiciary. Conversely, if the entire administrative success starts to depend on the willpower of a single person, the long-term stability of such a system may be questioned.

The questions that need to be answered by the Balen government are clear. Who ordered the arrest of the journalist and what was the legal justification for it? What is the factual basis for the different explanations from the Prime Minister’s Secretariat and the police? What was the objective basis for changing the role of the Inspector General of Police? Was there political interference in the investigation involving people close to power? When will a clear practice of holding the Prime Minister accountable through regular questions and answers in Parliament be established? Answering these questions is not about weakening the government; it is an opportunity to strengthen public trust and institutional legitimacy.

Criticizing the government in a democracy is not about trying to make the government fail. The purpose of criticism is also to put pressure on it to correct wrong practices. Questioning the use of state power, journalists publishing news that is inconvenient for the government, MPs demanding answers from the Prime Minister, and police leadership having the legal basis of their decisions examined are natural processes in a democratic system. The government may be uncomfortable with these processes, but it is its responsibility to respect them.

Ultimately, the question of good governance is not limited to the personal disputes of any one Prime Minister, Minister, Journalist or Inspector General of Police. It is a question of what kind of governance culture to establish in Nepal. It is a question of whether the new political leadership will repeat the weaknesses of the old system or establish different institutional practices. The people can change the political leadership, but the responsibility to strengthen the constitutional institutions must be borne by the leadership itself.

Answering questions in parliament is good governance. Facing questions from journalists is good governance. Allowing the police to act according to the law is good governance. Respecting the rights of the opposition is good governance. Treating citizens who do not support you with equal respect is good governance. Being ready to correct your own decisions if they are wrong is also good governance. Good governance is not just the ability to discipline others, but also the commitment to keep your power under the discipline of the constitution and the law.

The main question that needs to be asked of the Balen government now is this – is the character of governance changing with the change in power, or is the old tendency to use state power under the new slogan of good governance continuing? No Facebook status, political speech or propaganda campaign will answer this. The government's decision-making process, institutional behavior and public accountability will provide it. Because ultimately, the true identity of good governance in a democracy is not determined by how powerful the government is, but by how justly, legitimately and responsibly that power is used.
